title: Sub-row-group scan morsels for tables with few row groups
summary: Parallel table scans can now hand out pieces of a row group (morsels) instead of always handing out a whole row group (~122k rows) per task. I added a static helper, RowGroupCollection::GetParallelScanMorselVectors(total_rows, row_group_size, threads). It aims for about 4 morsels per thread, uses at least 4 vectors (8k rows) per morsel, and never more than one row group. RowGroupCollection::NextParallelScan now uses the existing sub-row-group branch whenever the morsel is smaller than the current row group, or when it is part-way through a row group. That branch was previously only used under verify_parallelism, which still gets 1 vector. It advances vector_index by the morsel size and adds the morsel's own rows to processed_rows. DataTable::MaxThreads uses the same helper, so the scan source starts enough threads. I put the helper in row_group_collection.hpp rather than scan_state.hpp, so ParallelCollectionScanState is unchanged. The morsel size is recomputed under the lock on every call, which is a few arithmetic operations. Results: the build is OK and bench reported no result mismatches. q02 went from 88.7 to 72.3 ms (-18.5%) on the first run and from 91.2 to 79.0 ms (-13.4%) on the second. Before the change, the profile showed the 100k-row supplier scan taking 0.02s on a single thread.
notes:
- MaxThreads uses GetTotalRows(), while NextParallelScan uses max_row minus the base row id fixed at scan start. The two can differ slightly if rows are appended during a scan, but that only affects the thread-count estimate, not correctness.
- Under verify_parallelism, processed_rows is now updated as well; before, it was never updated in that mode.
- Not measured in isolation: whether scanning from a vector offset inside compressed or FSST string segments costs extra. The end-to-end time improved anyway.
- Possible follow-ups: tune MORSELS_PER_THREAD and MIN_MORSEL_VECTORS, and check that the 17-row-group part scan (now about 31-vector morsels) is balanced.

title: Sparse Select for BitPacking segments (decode only selected rows)
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q02 +2.2%; needs at least -5%)
summary:
I added a `select` callback for BitpackingSelect in src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp and registered it in GetBitpackingFunction. With it, StandardColumnData::Select now takes its specialised path for bitpacked columns that have constant validity, where before it fell back to Scan plus Slice.
- **Sparse selections** (sel_count*4 <= vector_count and sel ascending): the scan walks to each selected row and reads the single value. CONSTANT and CONSTANT_DELTA values are computed directly. For FOR and DELTA_FOR it unpacks only the 32-value algorithm group holding the row. For FOR groups the unpacked group is cached and reused by neighbouring rows, keyed on group pointer and width.
- **Dense selections**, or a vector that starts in a DELTA_FOR group: the vector is decoded with BitpackingScanPartial and the selected rows are gathered in place. This is safe because sel[i] >= i when sel is ascending. If sel is not ascending, it decodes into a scratch vector instead.
- **Scan position:** a helper, BitpackingSelectAdvance, moves the scan state the same way a scan would. It does not load the next metadata group when a skip ends exactly on a group boundary, so it never reads past the last group of a segment.

**Result:** `bench` shows q02 at 73.7 ms before and 65.6 ms after (-11.0%), with results checked equal. That is about half the 15-25% the issue predicted.

**Correctness checks:** on persisted lineitem and orders I compared queries using a pushed WHERE filter (sparse selections) against the same aggregates written with FILTER clauses over full scans (no pushdown), covering BIGINT, DECIMAL, DATE and INTEGER columns at about 0.15%, 1.3% and about 20% selectivity. Each hash or sum pair matched. I could not run the bitpacking sqllogic tests: the only shell command allowed is dbe-tool, which has no test runner.
notes: The bitpacking Skip() loads the next metadata group whenever a skip ends exactly on a 1024-row group boundary. At the end of a segment that would read past the last group. That is why BitpackingSelectAdvance steps the last row by hand. Watch for this in any future caller of Skip. If a DELTA_FOR group is entered partway through a vector, the sparse path stays correct, because Skip decodes and carries current_delta_offset, but it is not faster there. Follow-up idea: a selective validity select for non-constant (uncompressed) validity would let nullable bitpacked columns use the same fast path.

title: Compact sparse filtered scan output into fuller chunks within a morsel
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I added sparse-chunk compaction to the parallel DuckTableScanState::TableScanFunc in src/function/table/table_scan.cpp, but it gave no measurable speedup on q02, so I'm abandoning it.

How it worked: when a scan chunk had fewer than STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/8 rows, it was copied with DataChunk::Append into a per-thread compact_buffer. The scan kept going within the same morsel until the buffer held at least STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE/2 rows or the morsel ran out, then the buffer was returned. Details:
- A chunk that would overflow the buffer was stored in a compact_pending chunk and returned on the next call.
- A morsel_exhausted flag made the next call go straight to NextParallelScan.
- The batch index was recorded when buffering started and returned by TableScanGetPartitionData. This was needed because CollectionScanState::Scan sets row_group to nullptr at the end of a morsel, so the normal lookup would give the wrong batch index for the last buffered chunk.
- Index-creation scans were left unchanged. Full chunks with an empty buffer were returned without copying.

Results: it built OK and the q02 results matched. Seven `bench q02` runs gave +4.8%, -1.6%, -8.9%, -3.6%, -7.0%, -0.5% and +7.0%, a mean of about -1.4%. That is well inside the ±5% noise and short of the 5% bar. In the profile, the first hash-join probe after the partsupp scan (the p_partkey join) still shows about 0.01s, the same as before.
notes:
- q02 total time is about 47–57ms hot, and run-to-run noise is ±7%. Anything that saves only a few milliseconds of summed CPU across threads cannot pass the 5% bar on this template.
- The profile's per-operator times for the first probe after the sparse partsupp scan (0.01–0.03s) are summed across threads. That overstates the wall-time gain available from removing per-chunk overhead.
- If anyone tries compaction again: at the end of a morsel, CollectionScanState::Scan sets table_state.row_group to nullptr. Any buffering across Scan calls must therefore save the batch index before that happens, or batch and insertion order breaks.
- The larger costs in the q02 profile are elsewhere: the supplier scan at 0.06s, the s_suppkey hash join at 0.02s, and the CTE and delim join at 0.01s each.

title: Row-level execution of small dynamic IN filters behind a selectivity guard
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: I implemented the plan and it builds, but it gives no speedup, so I'm abandoning it. Changes: (1) PushInFilter wraps IN-lists of at most 16 values with a numeric/varchar physical type in a SelectivityOptionalFilter (threshold 0.5, 30 check vectors) instead of a plain OptionalFilter. (2) ColumnSegment::FilterSelection gets a typed IN_FILTER case. (3) TableFilterState::Initialize gets IN_FILTER support (empty state). (4) ConstantFun::FiltersNullValues gets IN_FILTER support (filters NULLs). Effect in q02.m0: the supplier TABLE_SCAN now emits 20,051 rows instead of about 96k, but its cumulative time stays at 0.07s. Bench: q02 52.1ms best vs 53.0ms mine (+1.8%, noise). Root cause: the issue assumed the unfiltered scan decompresses every FSST string. It doesn't. FSSTStorage::StringScan emits lazy FSST_VECTORs, while the filtered path (FSSTStorage::Select) decompresses eagerly. Direct check on the 100k-row table, s_name and s_phone only: unfiltered scan 0.02s, scan with a strict 20%-selective filter (s_nationkey<5) 0.03s. Adding all 7 columns with a strict selective filter still gives 0.06s. So early row filtering does not make this scan cheaper.
notes:
- Dead end: filtering rows early to save string decompression does not work for FSST columns. A full scan already emits lazy FSST vectors; the Select path decompresses eagerly. Check compression with pragma_storage_info and compare filtered vs unfiltered scan time with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before proposing ideas like this.
- The supplier scan cost (about 0.06s cumulative for 100k rows, 7 columns, one row group) is not proportional to rows selected. Something per-vector or per-morsel probably dominates. One candidate: FSST StartScan delta-decodes offsets from the segment start whenever a new morsel begins mid-segment (last_known_row resets on a fresh scan state), and sub-row-group morsels (commit E0001) make that happen more often. Another: the 12 uncompressed string segments. Worth profiling.
- Side finding: RowGroup::CheckZonemap marks top-level OPTIONAL_FILTERs as always-true. A SelectivityOptionalFilter only runs on rows when it sits inside a CONJUNCTION_AND, which happens here because min/max filters are pushed alongside.
- The IN_FILTER FilterSelection, Initialize and FiltersNullValues cases are correct and could be reused if row-level IN filtering is wanted elsewhere. BOOL was left out (std::vector<bool> doesn't compile in the typed loop, and a two-value bool list is always dense anyway).

title: Raise selectivity ratio required to materialize a common multi-table subplan
reasons: no visible template faster beyond its noise (best: q02 +1.6%; needs at least -5%)
summary: I changed one constant in CommonSubplanFinder::IsSelectiveMultiTablePlan (src/optimizer/common_subplan_optimizer.cpp:977): CARDINALITY_RATIO goes from 2 to 8. A non-aggregate multi-table subplan estimated above 2048 rows is now materialized only if its estimate is below 1/8 of its largest base table. The 2048 threshold and the aggregate/distinct path are unchanged. The tree builds (BUILD OK). EXPLAIN ANALYZE of q02.m0 confirms the __common_subplan CTE is gone (the baseline plan in .dbe/profile.md has it). supplier⋈nation⋈region is now computed separately in the outer query and in the decorrelated min() subquery, with direct table-scan build sides and dynamic filters on supplier and partsupp. Results matched in every bench run. Six bench runs on q02 (best vs mine, ms): 49.9→47.9 (-4.1%), 52.6→55.0 (+4.7%), 51.5→48.1 (-6.5%), 55.2→42.8 (-22.5%), 51.7→48.7 (-5.9%), 49.1→46.6 (-5.1%). The median is about -5.5%, much less than the -20 to -25% the issue predicted. The baseline ran at about 50 ms in bench, not the 68 ms the hypothesis measured, so the barrier costs less than estimated in this harness. The gain is real but small and noisy, close to the 5% bar.
notes: The issue predicted 68→50 ms, but the harness baseline is already about 50 ms, so the measured gain is only about 5% (median of 6 runs) and noisy, with one run at +4.7% and one at -22.5%. Without the CTE the join order looks the same as the baseline's CTE body: supplier probes the nation⋈region build, and partsupp probes part. So the gain comes from removing the barrier and the copy, not from a different join order. In the new plan the time goes mainly to the partsupp scan (~0.14s cumulative across threads), the part scan with its suffix filter (0.05s) and the supplier scan (0.06s). Follow-up: the decorrelated subquery side still rescans partsupp and supplier; sharing one partsupp scan between the outer side and the min() side is a possible next step.

title: Rewrite correlated MIN/MAX scalar subquery over a subset of the outer join into a window aggregate
summary:
I added a WinMagic-style unnesting rewrite to `src/planner/binder/query_node/plan_select_node.cpp`. It is about 300 lines in an anonymous-namespace `SubqueryToWindowRewriter`, called at the start of `Binder::PlanFilter`. No header changes. The rewrite fires when one WHERE conjunct contains exactly one correlated scalar subquery and all of these hold:
- The subquery plan is a projection of an ungrouped `min`/`max` (one argument, no DISTINCT, FILTER or ORDER BY) over cross products, filters and table scans.
- The outer FROM is the same kind of tree.
- Each subquery scan maps to a distinct outer scan of the same table (same catalog entry and function, no table or dynamic filters, no ordinality), and every column the subquery uses is projected by that outer scan.
- Every remapped subquery conjunct equals an outer conjunct (flipped comparisons count as equal).
- The outer conjuncts left unmatched reference only the extra outer scans.
- Every correlated column has depth 1, belongs to an extra outer scan, appears directly in a matched equality (which rejects NULLs) and has a type that partitions exactly: integral, boolean, varchar, date, timestamp, decimal or uuid. Floats and nested types are refused.
- Nothing is volatile and no other conjunct holds a subquery.

The plan then becomes Filter(other conjuncts) → Window(min/max(remapped argument) OVER (PARTITION BY correlated columns, whole partition)) → Filter(original conjunct with the subquery replaced by the window column). If any check fails, nothing is touched and the existing delim-join decorrelation runs.

Measured with `dbe-tool bench`, against the current best, results checked: q02 went from 51.7 to 29.7 ms (-42.5%) in one run and from 58.2 to 35.2 ms (-39.6%) in a full-bench run. EXPLAIN shows the LEFT_DELIM_JOIN, the second partsupp scan and the hash aggregate gone, replaced by one WINDOW over the 5-way join.

Edge cases I ran on temp tables, with results checked by hand:
- Duplicate keys in the extra table: min and max are unaffected.
- NULL correlated keys and NULL aggregate values.
- A comparison written in flipped orientation.
- IS NOT DISTINCT FROM correlation: falls back.
- An extra outer conjunct on a matched table: falls back, result empty as expected.
- Self-join with the same table twice: falls back.
- Two correlated columns: rewritten, partitions by both.
- A correlated column inside the aggregate argument with no equality on it: falls back.
- Empty input, and `count` instead of min/max: not rewritten.
notes:
- The rewrite sits in the binder, in `PlanFilter` before `PlanSubqueries`. At that point the WHERE conjuncts are still a single expression and the FROM is a raw cross-product tree, which makes the subset matching simple.
- Scan matching is greedy: the first unused outer scan on the same table. A different assignment that would also work can be missed, but that only costs a fallback, never correctness.
- Possible follow-ups:
  - Extend to correlation without an equality, partitioning on all correlated columns. The earlier argument shows it is sound for exact-equality partitioning; it was left out to stay strict.
  - Allow outer joins written with explicit `JOIN ... ON`. They are bound as comparison joins, so they currently fall back.
  - Apply the same idea to EXISTS / IN subsets.
- No dead ends. The first build worked and the gain matched or beat the hand rewrite measured in the issue (it promised about -20%).
